usage: Used when something sounds familiar, even if you cannot remember all the specific details.
common_mistakes: It rings me a bell (incorrect object placement)
example_sentences: The name 'John Smith' rings a bell, but I'm not sure if I've met him.
Have you been to the new cafe? - The name rings a bell, but I haven't been yet.
Does this address ring a bell to you?
I'm not certain, but that story rings a bell.
The tune rings a bell, though I can't place the song.
native_notes: This is a fixed idiom. Never change the word 'ring' to 'sound' or 'play'.

uzbek: biri bilan uchrashib yangiliklarni muhokama qilmoq
usage: Used when meeting friends or colleagues after a period of time to share news and life updates.
common_mistakes: catching up with news (usually implies people)
example_sentences: It was great to catch up with my old school friends last night.
We should grab a coffee soon and catch up with everything.
I haven't seen Sam in months; I really need to catch up with him.
After the exam, we all caught up with each other over dinner.
Let's meet at the cafe to catch up with all the latest gossip.
native_notes: Very common in social settings. 'Catch up on' is used for work or tasks, while 'catch up with' is for people.

usage: Used when something sounds familiar but you cannot remember the exact details or context.
alternatives: I think I've heard that before
example_sentences: The name Sarah Miller rings a bell, but I can't quite place her.
Does the address 12 Oak Street ring a bell?
When he mentioned the incident, it vaguely rang a bell.
I’ve never been there before, but the place name rings a bell.
His voice rings a bell, but I don't know where we met.
collocations: doesn't ring a bell at all
native_notes: This is an idiomatic expression. It signifies that your brain recognizes the information, but you lack full recall.

usage: Used in British English to suggest an activity or ask if someone wants to do something.
common_mistakes: do you fancy to go (must be V-ing)
example_sentences: Do you fancy grabbing a pizza later tonight?
I fancy seeing that new film at the cinema this weekend.
Do you fancy going for a walk in the park?
She doesn't really fancy cooking dinner tonight.
Do you fancy a quick drink after work?
native_notes: Extremely common in the UK. It sounds much more natural and friendly than 'Do you want to...'.

uzbek: esimdan chiqib ketdi, kallam ishlamay qoldi
usage: Used when you are under pressure (like an exam or presentation) and suddenly cannot remember information.
common_mistakes: I had a blank mind (wrong structure)
alternatives: I can't recall at the moment
example_sentences: I walked into the exam, and suddenly my mind went blank.
I was so nervous during the interview that my mind went blank.
Don't worry if your mind goes blank; just take a deep breath.
I tried to remember the password, but my mind went blank.
I know the answer, but my mind just went blank for a second.
collocations: panic made my mind go blank
native_notes: A great expression to explain a momentary loss of memory, very useful during IELTS Speaking if you get stuck.

usage: Used when you want to show someone an idea or plan to see if they approve or have feedback.
example_sentences: I have an idea for the presentation, can I run it by you?
Before I send this email, I need to run it by my manager.
Do you have a second? I'd like to run something by you.
It's a good plan, but you should run it by the team first.
She likes to run every major decision by her mentor.
native_notes: Excellent for professional contexts where collaboration is required. Sounds much more natural than 'ask for an opinion'.

usage: Used when something sounds familiar, even if you can't quite remember the details.
alternatives: I have a vague recollection of that
example_sentences: The name Sarah Jenkins rings a bell, but I can't place where I know her from.
Does the title of this book ring a bell?
When he mentioned the accident, it started to ring a bell.
I’ve never met him, but his face rings a bell.
That melody really rings a bell, but I don't know the song name.
native_notes: Very common in spoken English. It conveys a partial memory rather than full recognition.

expression: A bit of a long shot
usage: Used when describing something that is unlikely to succeed or happen.
grammar_pattern: It is a bit of a long shot
example_sentences: Asking for a promotion right now is a bit of a long shot.
It's a long shot, but we could try calling them one more time.
Winning the lottery is always a bit of a long shot.
I know it's a long shot, but do you have an extra ticket?
Getting into that university is a bit of a long shot with my current grades.
native_notes: Often used when someone is still willing to try despite the low odds.

expression: Hit the nail on the head
usage: Used when someone describes exactly what is causing a situation or problem.
grammar_pattern: You/That + hit the nail on the head
common_mistakes: Hit the nail in the head
Hit the head on the nail
example_sentences: You hit the nail on the head when you said the team lacks communication.
That's exactly why we're failing—you hit the nail on the head.
She hit the nail on the head regarding the management issues.
I think he really hit the nail on the head with his analysis of the market.
You’ve hit the nail on the head; that’s precisely the core of the problem.
collocations: totally hit the nail on the head
really hit the nail on the head
hit the nail on the head about
native_notes: A very idiomatic, high-level way to agree with someone's accurate observation.

uzbek: biri bilan uchrashib yangiliklardan xabardor bo'lmoq
usage: Used when you meet someone you haven't seen for a while to talk about what has been happening in your lives.
example_sentences: It’s been ages; we really need to catch up with each other soon.
I spent the whole afternoon catching up with my old school friends.
Let’s grab a coffee and catch up with all the news.
I need to catch up with my emails after being away for a week.
We caught up with the latest gossip during our lunch break.
native_notes: Very common in both British and American English. It implies a sense of missing time that needs to be filled.

uzbek: biror narsani kimdir bilan maslahatlashib olish yoki tasdiqlatish
usage: Used when you want to tell someone your idea or plan to see if they agree or have any feedback.
common_mistakes: run by me that idea (wrong word order)
example_sentences: I have a quick idea; can I run it by you?
I need to run the budget proposal by my manager before we send it.
Could you run that plan by the rest of the team first?
Don't worry, I’ll run it by Sarah to see what she thinks.
I just wanted to run a thought by you before making a decision.
native_notes: Highly idiomatic. It suggests a collaborative and respectful approach to decision-making.

usage: Used to describe being away from home, usually doing chores, running errands, or simply socialising in public.
common_mistakes: I am out and in (incorrect idiom)
I am going to out and about (incorrect usage of 'to')
example_sentences: I've been out and about all day, so I'm absolutely exhausted.
Are you going to be out and about this weekend?
We were just out and about when we bumped into an old friend.
It feels good to be out and about after staying inside all week.
If you're out and about, could you pick up some milk?
native_notes: Very British-sounding and very common in casual conversation.

usage: Used when you are struggling to reach a decision and finally do so.
example_sentences: I still haven't made up my mind about which university to apply to.
It took me a while, but I finally made up my mind to go.
She made up her mind instantly.
Once I make up my mind, nothing can change it.
Have you made up your mind yet?
collocations: hard to make up one's mind
unable to make up one's mind
native_notes: Stronger than just 'deciding'; it emphasizes the process of choosing after a period of doubt or consideration.

expression: to make a point of doing something
uzbek: atayin biror narsa qilmoq / shuni odat qilmoq
usage: Used when you deliberately ensure you do something because you think it is important.
grammar_pattern: Subject + make a point of + V-ing
example_sentences: I make a point of reading for an hour every night.
She makes a point of thanking every customer personally.
The director makes a point of checking in with staff regularly.
Always make a point of double-checking your work before submitting.
They make a point of eating dinner together as a family.
native_notes: Shows intent and deliberate action rather than just a habit.

uzbek: vaziyatga qarab ish tutmoq / oldindan rejalashtirmay harakat qilmoq
usage: Used when you don't have a firm plan and will decide how to act based on how a situation develops.
example_sentences: I'm not sure how long the meeting will take, so let's play it by ear.
We don't have a strict itinerary; we'll just play it by ear.
Do you want to book a restaurant, or should we play it by ear?
Don't worry about the plan; we can play it by ear depending on the weather.
They decided to play it by ear regarding the start date.
collocations: decided to play it by ear
native_notes: Originates from musicians who play music without reading sheet music; implies flexibility.

usage: A polite and standard way to offer or ask for help.
common_mistakes: Give a hand to him (word order is awkward)
Give me a hand with help (redundant)
example_sentences: Could you give me a hand with these heavy boxes?
I'd be happy to give you a hand with your presentation.
Thanks for giving me a hand earlier today.
If you're stuck, just give me a hand.
He gave me a hand moving the furniture into the new flat.
native_notes: Very British-friendly. 'Lend a hand' is a slightly more idiomatic variant of this.

uzbek: biror nima qilmoqchi bo'lmoq / nima qilib yuribsan?
usage: Used to ask what someone is doing or to describe someone's current activities/intentions.
grammar_pattern: Subject + be + up to + verb-ing / noun
common_mistakes: What are you up to do? (incorrect structure)
I am up to studying (not used for routine)
example_sentences: What have you been up to lately?
I'm not sure what to do today, what are you up to?
They look suspicious, I wonder what they're up to.
I've been up to my neck in revision for the IELTS test.
Whatever you're up to, make sure you're back by eight.
native_notes: Often used in the phrase 'What are you up to?' as a casual greeting, or 'up to no good' to imply mischief.

usage: Use this to politely admit that you forgot to do something or forgot an appointment.
common_mistakes: It slipped out of my mind (incorrect idiom)
I forgot it from my mind (redundant)
alternatives: It went straight out of my head
example_sentences: I am so sorry, it completely slipped my mind to pay the bill.
It slipped my mind that today was your birthday, happy belated birthday!
Did you pick up the milk? Oh, it slipped my mind entirely.
I meant to send you the file, but it slipped my mind during the busy morning.
Don't worry, it happens; things often slip my mind when I'm stressed.
native_notes: This is a softer, more socially acceptable way to say 'I forgot', as it implies it was an accidental lapse rather than a lack of caring.

usage: Use this to say that someone's guess, opinion, or performance is exactly right.
common_mistakes: Your answer is very spot on (don't use intensifiers like 'very' as it is already emphatic)
That was a spot on (missing 'a' if used as adjective before noun)
alternatives: to be bang on the money
to hit the nail on the head
example_sentences: Your assessment of the situation was spot on.
The weather forecast for today was spot on; it didn't rain at all.
His impression of the manager was absolutely spot on.
I think your advice about changing jobs was spot on.
Is the timing for the meeting okay? Yes, that's spot on.
native_notes: Very common in both British and Australian English to express strong agreement with someone's accuracy.

usage: Used when someone decides to try a new activity or task, often despite being uncertain about the outcome.
common_mistakes: Give a go it (wrong word order)
Give it for a go (incorrect preposition)
example_sentences: I've never played tennis before, but I'm willing to give it a go.
Why don't you give cooking a go this weekend?
It looks difficult, but I’ll give it a go anyway.
I wasn't sure if I could fix the bike, but I decided to give it a go.
You should definitely give the new Italian restaurant a go.
collocations: decide to give it a go
native_notes: Extremely idiomatic British English. It sounds much more casual and confident than the standard 'try'.

usage: Used to express interest or willingness to participate in a suggested plan or activity.
common_mistakes: I am up to go to the cinema (incorrect preposition)
I up for the movie (missing verb 'to be')
alternatives: to be in the mood for
example_sentences: Are you up for going out tonight?
I’m not really up for a party; I’d rather just relax at home.
If you're up for a long walk, let's head to the park.
Is anyone up for a game of cards?
I'm totally up for trying that new Indian place.
native_notes: Sounds very natural and conversational. It is slightly more 'active' and 'social' than simply saying 'I want to'.

usage: A very British way to express frustration or annoyance about something recurring.
common_mistakes: Changing the pronoun (e.g., 'it does head in me')
Using it in a formal essay
example_sentences: This constant rain is really doing my head in.
The noise from the neighbours is starting to do my head in.
Doing these repetitive tasks all day really does my head in.
Don't talk about that again, it's doing my head in!
His constant complaining is doing my head in.
collocations: starts to do my head in
native_notes: Pure British slang. Do not use this in formal writing or IELTS Speaking if aiming for a very neutral register.

expression: to make a go of it
uzbek: urinib ko'rmoq / muvaffaqiyatga erishishga harakat qilmoq
usage: Used when someone decides to try their best to make a venture, relationship, or situation successful.
example_sentences: They decided to open a cafe and really make a go of it.
It's a difficult business, but I’m determined to make a go of it.
We didn't get off to a good start, but we're trying to make a go of it.
Moving abroad was tough, but we managed to make a go of it.
If you want to make a go of your career, you need to work hard.
collocations: make a real go of it
trying to make a go of it
determined to make a go of it
native_notes: Implies persistence despite initial difficulties or skepticism.

expression: I'm tied up at the moment
usage: Used when you cannot deal with someone or a task immediately because you are busy with something else.
grammar_pattern: Subject + be (conjugated) + tied up + at the moment
common_mistakes: I am very busy at the moment (a bit repetitive)
alternatives: I'm flat out at the moment
example_sentences: I'm tied up at the moment, can I call you back in an hour?
Sorry, I'm tied up at the moment with this report.
Could you wait a minute? I'm completely tied up at the moment.
I'd love to help, but I'm tied up at the moment.
She's tied up at the moment dealing with a client issue.
native_notes: Much more common and natural than saying 'I am very busy'. It sounds professional yet casual.

usage: A polite, idiomatic way to admit you forgot something important.
alternatives: It went straight out of my head
example_sentences: I'm so sorry, it completely slipped my mind to pay the bill.
I meant to send you that email, but it slipped my mind.
Did you pick up the milk? Oh no, it slipped my mind!
It slipped my mind that today was a public holiday.
My apologies, it slipped my mind during the busy morning.
native_notes: Used when you genuinely intended to do something but simply forgot. It sounds less irresponsible than saying 'I forgot'.

usage: A friendly, casual way to say goodbye to friends or colleagues.
example_sentences: I have to run to class now, catch you later!
Catch you later, let me know how the interview goes.
Nice chatting with you, catch you later!
I'm heading out now, catch you later tonight.
We're off to the cinema, catch you later!
native_notes: Strictly informal. Do not use this in an IELTS Speaking test, as it is too casual.

usage: A polite and common way to state that you do not like a specific activity or hobby.
grammar_pattern: Subject + be + not + really + into + noun/gerund
alternatives: It's not my cup of tea
example_sentences: Do you want to go to the jazz concert? Honestly, I'm not really into it.
I tried rock climbing, but I'm not really into it.
Some people love horror films, but I'm not really into them.
He keeps asking me to play golf, but I'm not really into it.
Cooking is fine, but I'm not really into it as a hobby.
collocations: not really into it at all
opposites: I'm a big fan of it
native_notes: Very versatile. It is much more idiomatic than saying 'I do not like this'.

usage: A standard, welcoming phrase used when someone visits your house or workspace.
alternatives: Please, come in and sit down
example_sentences: Come in! Make yourself at home while I put the kettle on.
Don't stand on ceremony, just make yourself at home.
Please, make yourself at home and help yourself to a drink.
I hope you can make yourself at home in our guest room.
They made us feel very welcome and told us to make ourselves at home.
collocations: feel free to make yourself at home
warmly told to make yourself at home
native_notes: Crucial for hospitality. Often accompanied by 'don't stand on ceremony' for extra politeness.

usage: Used when you cannot accept an invitation or meet someone because you have other commitments.
common_mistakes: I am busy at tied up
alternatives: I've got a lot on my plate
example_sentences: I'd love to help you move house, but I'm tied up all Saturday.
Can we talk later? I'm a bit tied up with a project deadline right now.
Sorry, I can't make it to the cinema; I'm tied up at the office.
He's usually tied up in meetings until late afternoon.
I'm tied up dealing with these emails at the moment.
native_notes: Much more common and natural than saying 'I am very busy'. It implies that you are physically or mentally constrained by tasks.

usage: Used to hedge a statement or make it less precise/direct in casual conversation.
example_sentences: I'm sort of tired after that long flight.
Did you enjoy the concert? Yeah, sort of, but it was too loud.
He's sort of acting like he's the boss around here.
We're sort of planning to go to Italy this summer.
Are you annoyed with me? Sort of, but not really.
native_notes: Often pronounced 'sorta' in speech. It is a classic filler that softens an opinion.

usage: Used when learning a new skill that initially felt difficult but is now becoming easier.
example_sentences: Driving a manual car is tricky, but I'm starting to get the hang of it.
At first, the software was confusing, but I think I’ve got the hang of it now.
Don't worry, you'll get the hang of the new system within a week.
I’ve finally got the hang of making sushi at home.
It takes time to get the hang of speaking a new language.
collocations: finally get the hang of it
starting to get the hang of it
quickly get the hang of it
hard to get the hang of
never get the hang of it
native_notes: Extremely idiomatic. It conveys progress and successful adjustment after a period of struggle.

uzbek: biri bilan uchrashib yangiliklardan xabardor bo'lmoq
usage: Used when you meet a friend you haven't seen in a while to hear about what they have been doing.
example_sentences: It’s been ages! We really need to catch up with each other soon.
I met my old classmate yesterday to catch up with all the news.
Let's grab lunch next week and catch up with things.
Whenever I visit home, I try to catch up with all my childhood friends.
It was great to catch up with her over a glass of wine.
native_notes: Note the preposition 'with'. Using it without 'with' is a common error among learners.

expression: to be a bit of a stretch
uzbek: biroz bo'rttirilgan yoki haqiqatdan yiroq bo'lmoq
usage: Used when something is unlikely to be true or is slightly beyond the limits of credibility.
grammar_pattern: It + be + a bit of a stretch + (to V / that clause)
alternatives: it's a bit of an exaggeration
example_sentences: Calling that tiny flat a 'luxury penthouse' is a bit of a stretch.
To say he is the best player in the world is a bit of a stretch.
It's a bit of a stretch to suggest that the plan will work without any funding.
Claiming the project is finished when we have weeks of work left is a bit of a stretch.
Maybe that's a bit of a stretch, don't you think?
native_notes: This is a polite way to disagree with someone's claim without being rude.

usage: Used when watching something or someone to ensure they are safe or functioning correctly.
example_sentences: Could you keep an eye on my bag while I go to the restroom?
I need to keep an eye on the oven so the cake doesn't burn.
The doctor wants to keep an eye on his blood pressure for a few days.
Can you keep an eye on the kids while I make dinner?
I'm just keeping an eye on the news to see if the weather improves.
collocations: keep an eye on the time
keep an eye on the situation
native_notes: Idiomatic expression. 'Keep an eye out for' is different and means to watch for something specific to appear.

usage: Used when your supply of something is completely finished.
example_sentences: We've run out of milk, so can you pick some up on your way back?
I'm afraid we've run out of time to finish the presentation.
The bakery ran out of fresh bread within an hour of opening.
I don't want to run out of money while I'm travelling.
We almost ran out of fuel before finding a petrol station.
native_notes: Very common in IELTS Speaking Part 1 when discussing daily routines or habits.

usage: Used to confirm that something is logical, reasonable, or easy to understand.
example_sentences: That makes sense; I never thought of it that way.
It makes sense to start early so we can avoid the traffic.
Does that make sense, or would you like me to explain it again?
It makes sense that they would be tired after such a long flight.
I suppose that makes sense under the current circumstances.
native_notes: Use 'It makes sense' rather than 'It is logical' to sound more natural in casual discussion.

usage: Used when dealing with a problem, organizing something messy, or fixing a situation.
example_sentences: I need to sort out my schedule before the weekend starts.
We need to sort out the logistics for the conference next month.
Don't worry, I'll sort out the hotel reservations for us.
It took a while, but we finally managed to sort out the disagreement.
I've got a few things to sort out at home before I can join you.
native_notes: In British English, this is the go-to phrase for 'fixing' or 'organizing' almost anything.

uzbek: bu menga yoqmaydi, bu mening didim emas
usage: Used to describe something you do not particularly like or are not interested in, without being overly harsh.
grammar_pattern: [Subject] is not my cup of tea
common_mistakes: It is not my tea cup.
It is not cup of tea for me.
example_sentences: Thanks for the invite, but modern art is not really my cup of tea.
Horror films aren't exactly my cup of tea.
Jazz music is not my cup of tea, I prefer rock.
Actually, spicy food is not my cup of tea.
I don't mind the office, but the commute is not my cup of tea.
collocations: definitely not my cup of tea
really not my cup of tea
a bit of a cup of tea
not exactly my cup of tea
native_notes: Very British-sounding idiom; extremely common in casual conversation to express a preference without offending.

usage: Used when you are struggling to decide between options or finally reaching a decision.
example_sentences: I haven't been able to make up my mind about which course to take.
It's hard to make up my mind when there are so many options.
Once I make up my mind, nothing can change it.
Take your time to make up your mind.
He finally made up his mind to quit his job.
collocations: hard to make up my mind
struggle to make up my mind
native_notes: Slightly more personal and process-oriented than the formal 'decide'.

usage: Used when giving a rough estimate rather than an exact, precise number.
grammar_pattern: to give a ballpark figure (for something)
example_sentences: I don't know the exact cost, but could you give me a ballpark figure?
That's just a ballpark figure; the real price might be higher.
He gave us a ballpark figure of how many guests might attend.
Can you provide a ballpark figure for the total renovation?
It's hard to say, but as a ballpark figure, I'd suggest fifty pounds.
native_notes: Very common in work contexts or when planning costs (renovation, travel, budget).

uzbek: qisqa vaqtga tashrif buyurmoq / tezda kirib chiqmoq
usage: Used when you are visiting a place for a very short period because you are in a rush.
grammar_pattern: to make a flying visit (to a place)
common_mistakes: Doing a flying visit (usually 'make' is preferred)
example_sentences: I can only make a flying visit to London this weekend for a wedding.
She made a flying visit to the office before catching her flight.
It was only a flying visit, so I didn't get to see much of the city.
He's making a flying visit to Paris next week on business.
Can you make a flying visit to see us tomorrow morning?
native_notes: Suggests urgency; implies the person is busy and has a tight schedule.

usage: Used to describe the process of choosing between options or deciding what to do.
grammar_pattern: Subject + make up + possessive pronoun + mind
common_mistakes: using 'decide' instead of the phrase in formal writing without checking level
example_sentences: I still haven't made up my mind about which university to apply to.
He found it hard to make up his mind because both options were good.
She finally made up her mind to quit her job and travel.
Don't rush me; I need time to make up my mind.
Has the board made up its mind yet?
collocations: hard to make up one's mind
struggle to make up one's mind
native_notes: More natural than the simple verb 'decide' when talking about a personal choice or a difficult dilemma.

usage: Used when meeting friends to talk about what has happened since you last saw them.
common_mistakes: Saying 'catch with' instead of 'catch up with'
Confusing it with 'catching up' on sleep
example_sentences: It's been ages, we really need to catch up with each other.
I went for lunch with Sarah just to catch up on all the gossip.
Let's meet for a drink so we can properly catch up.
I have a lot of catching up to do with my family back home.
Whenever I visit London, I make sure to catch up with my old school friends.
native_notes: Includes the nuance of closing the gap in information since the last interaction.

usage: Used when you are starting to learn or understand how to do something that was previously difficult.
example_sentences: At first, the new software was confusing, but I'm finally getting the hang of it.
Don't worry, you'll get the hang of driving soon enough.
I'm starting to get the hang of speaking Uzbek, though it's tough.
He didn't know how to use the chopsticks, but he soon got the hang of them.
It takes a little time to get the hang of the local bus routes.
collocations: starting to get the hang of
hard to get the hang of
native_notes: Very idiomatic. It emphasizes the process of moving from confusion to competence.

uzbek: dam olmoq / o'zingni qiynama / xotirjam bo'l
usage: Used to tell someone to relax or not to worry, or as a way of saying goodbye.
example_sentences: You've been working too hard; you really need to take it easy this weekend.
Take it easy, there's no need to shout.
The doctor told him to take it easy while he recovers.
Anyway, I've got to go now. Take it easy!
Take it easy on the new guy; he's still learning.
native_notes: Multifunctional. Can be a command to relax or a casual farewell similar to 'have a good day'.

usage: Used when you are ready to leave a place or a social gathering.
common_mistakes: I'm going to make a movement (incorrect vocabulary)
example_sentences: It's getting late, I think it's time for me to make a move.
Thanks for the dinner, but I should really make a move now.
We're going to make a move before the traffic gets really bad.
Don't go yet! Can't you stay a bit longer? No, I really have to make a move.
We'll make a move right after the match finishes.
native_notes: More natural than 'I am leaving now'. It softens the departure, making it feel less abrupt.

usage: Used when you are considering different choices before making a final decision.
grammar_pattern: Subject + weigh up + the options / pros and cons
common_mistakes: I am weighing to the options (wrong verb usage)
I'm weighing the options up (grammatically okay, but less common)
alternatives: to consider the pros and cons
example_sentences: I need a few days to weigh up my options before accepting the job offer.
We are currently weighing up the options regarding the new marketing strategy.
Before you commit, it's worth weighing up the options carefully.
She spent all morning weighing up the options for her holiday destination.
Weighing up the options, it seems that moving house is the most sensible choice.
collocations: weigh up the pros and cons
native_notes: Sounds sophisticated and indicates a logical, measured approach to decision-making.

usage: Used to suggest that a claim or statement is not entirely true or is difficult to believe.
grammar_pattern: It is + a bit of a stretch + to say/that...
alternatives: That's a bit hard to believe
example_sentences: Calling that tiny flat 'luxurious' is a bit of a stretch.
To say he was the best student in the class is a bit of a stretch.
It's a bit of a stretch to assume everyone will agree with the plan.
That price tag is a bit of a stretch for my budget.
Saying the movie was perfect is a bit of a stretch, though it was good.
native_notes: Polite way to disagree with someone's exaggeration without being blunt or rude.
